Why mineral security matters for India

India requires reliable supplies of minerals and processed materials for electricity networks, transport, electronics, machinery, batteries, aerospace and other industries.

The challenge is not limited to discovering mineral deposits. A secure supply also requires economically viable extraction, suitable processing facilities, technical expertise, transport infrastructure, recycling and access to international markets.

India has therefore pursued policies addressing both the availability of mineral resources and the ability to convert them into useful industrial materials.

India's identification of critical minerals

The Ministry of Mines identified 30 critical minerals for India in 2023. The selection reflected India's economic and strategic requirements and concerns about mineral supply.

A related but different legal list was established through the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2023.

2 different figures must be distinguished: India's 2023 critical-mineral identification covered 30 minerals, while 24 critical and strategic minerals were placed in Part D of the First Schedule of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, as amended in 2023.

The 2023 amendment empowered the Central Government to auction mining leases and composite licences for specified critical and strategic minerals. A composite licence combines the right to undertake the prescribed prospecting and subsequent mining activities, subject to applicable conditions.

Thus, the number 30 relates to the identified national critical-mineral list, while 24 relates to the relevant statutory category. They are not interchangeable.

National Critical Mineral Mission

The Union Cabinet approved the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM) on 29 January 2025. The mission was approved to strengthen India's critical-mineral value chain and long-term supply security.

Its announced financial framework comprised:

  • ₹16,300 crore: Proposed government expenditure.
  • ₹18,000 crore: Expected investment from public sector undertakings and other stakeholders.
  • ₹34,300 crore: Combined announced financial framework over 7 years.

According to an official government statement dated 29 July 2025, the mission period is FY 2024–25 to FY 2030–31. These are announced expenditure and investment provisions, not figures establishing that the full amount had already been spent or invested.

What the mission seeks to strengthen

  • Domestic exploration: Identify and assess mineral resources within India, including suitable offshore areas.
  • Mining and beneficiation: Improve the availability of mineral-bearing material and its initial processing.
  • Refining and industrial processing: Develop capabilities to produce materials needed by manufacturing industries.
  • Recycling: Recover critical minerals from used products, manufacturing waste and other suitable materials.
  • Overseas access: Encourage access to mineral assets and reliable suppliers in other countries.
  • Research and resilience: Support technology development and proposed measures such as mineral-processing parks and strategic stockpiles.

Mission approval and implementation are different stages. The presence of a proposed processing park or stockpile in the mission does not establish that a particular facility was already operational by 14 November 2026.

KABIL and overseas mineral access

Khanij Bidesh India Limited (KABIL) was formed to help secure overseas sources of critical and strategic minerals for India.

It is a joint venture of National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO), Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL) and Mineral Exploration and Consultancy Limited (MECL).

KABIL's role concerns access to overseas mineral resources and related exploration or investment opportunities. Government statements have identified engagement with countries including Argentina and Australia. Its purpose should not be confused with the duties of a domestic geological survey organisation.

Gujarat's mineral and strategic-material connections

Mineral geography

Gujarat forms part of India's wider north-western mineral and industrial region. NCERT's account of Indian mineral geography identifies the Aravalli region extending through Rajasthan and part of Gujarat as an important mineral region. It also identifies bauxite deposits in the Bhavnagar and Jamnagar areas of Gujarat.

Bauxite is the principal ore used to produce aluminium. Aluminium is important for transport, electrical equipment, construction and manufacturing. However, an ordinary reference to bauxite deposits does not establish the presence of every critical mineral in the same location.

Kundol nickel and chromium block

The Ministry of Mines included the Kundol Nickel and Chromium Block in Gujarat among the 20 blocks announced in the first central auction tranche on 29 November 2023.

The official December 2023 announcement classified the Kundol block under a composite licence. This is a specific Gujarat connection to the national critical-mineral policy.

A mineral block being offered for auction is not proof of commercial production. The Kundol announcement identifies an auction-stage mineral block; it should not be interpreted as evidence that nickel or chromium was already being produced there.

National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing

India's manufacturing strategy is related to mineral and material security because new manufacturing methods need reliable supplies of suitable materials, equipment and skilled workers.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) released the National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing (NSAM) in February 2022.

Among its original stated objectives were development of 50 India-specific additive manufacturing technologies, support for 100 new start-ups, development of 500 new products and training of 100,000 skilled workers. These were strategy targets, not achievements at the date of launch.

In its report dated 7 October 2026, the Press Information Bureau stated that government-supported initiatives had trained more than 154,000 individuals, supported 56 additive manufacturing start-ups and developed 65 India-specific technologies. These figures are the government's reported progress as of that publication, not permanent totals.

The same October 2026 report described NSAM 2.0 as being conceptualised. This wording distinguishes the proposed next phase from a programme already completed.

Connecting manufacturing technology with mineral security

The subjects studied in this lesson are connected, but they solve different problems.

  • Additive manufacturing changes how suitable objects are produced and can reduce the need for separate parts in some designs.
  • Automation and smart manufacturing improve control, monitoring and coordination within industrial production.
  • Critical-mineral security addresses the reliability of materials needed by manufacturing and other essential sectors.

For example, a manufacturer producing an advanced electrical component may use a digitally controlled machine and robotic handling equipment. The machine may operate efficiently, but production can still be interrupted if a necessary metal or processed material is unavailable. Technological efficiency and material security are therefore complementary requirements.

Prelims focus

  • India identified 30 critical minerals in 2023; 24 critical and strategic minerals were listed in Part D of the First Schedule of the amended MMDR Act.
  • The Union Cabinet approved NCMM on 29 January 2025, with an announced combined financial framework of ₹34,300 crore over 7 years.
  • KABIL is a joint venture of NALCO, HCL and MECL.
  • Gujarat's Kundol Nickel and Chromium Block was included in the first auction tranche announced on 29 November 2023.
  • MeitY released NSAM in February 2022.
  • Trap: An announced target, auctioned block or proposed facility must not be treated as a completed achievement.

[Sources: Ministry of Mines, Press Information Bureau, Thirty Minerals Listed as Critical Minerals for India, including the first-auction annexure, 11 December 2023, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Mines, Press Information Bureau, Cabinet Approves National Critical Mineral Mission, 29 January 2025, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Heavy Industries, Press Information Bureau, Countering China's Curbs on Rare Earth Minerals, parliamentary reply on NCMM period and MMDR amendments, 29 July 2025, consulted 14 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Additive Manufacturing in India, sections National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing, Progress Under NSAM and NSAM 2.0, 7 October 2026, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 72–76.]

title: India's Critical Mineral Strategy, National Manufacturing Initiatives and Gujarat
